questions.question_text: What is the time complexity of accessing an element by index in an array?
questions.explanation: Arrays provide direct index-based access in constant time O(1) because elements are stored in contiguous memory locations.

questions.question_text: What is the worst-case time complexity of inserting an element at the beginning of a dynamic array?
questions.explanation: Inserting at the beginning requires shifting all existing elements one position to the right, resulting in O(n) time.

questions.question_text: Which operation is O(1) in a singly linked list with head pointer only?
questions.explanation: Insertion at the head requires creating a new node and updating the head pointer, both constant time operations.

questions.question_text: What is the main advantage of a doubly linked list over a singly linked list?
questions.explanation: Doubly linked lists maintain both next and previous pointers, enabling traversal in both directions.

questions.question_text: What is the maximum number of nodes at level k of a binary tree?
questions.explanation: At level k (root is level 0), a binary tree can have at most 2^k nodes since each node has at most 2 children.

questions.question_text: In a Red-Black tree, what is the maximum ratio of the longest path to the shortest path from root to a leaf?
questions.explanation: Red-Black trees guarantee that no path is more than twice as long as any other, maintaining the 2:1 ratio through color balancing rules.

questions.question_text: What is the average-case time complexity of a hash table lookup?
questions.explanation: Hash tables provide average-case O(1) lookup by computing a hash function to directly find the bucket.

questions.question_text: Which collision resolution technique can cause clustering and degrade hash table performance to O(n)?
questions.explanation: Linear probing causes primary clustering: consecutive occupied slots create long probe sequences, degrading to O(n) in the worst case.

questions.question_text: Which data structure follows the LIFO (Last In, First Out) principle?
questions.explanation: A stack follows LIFO — the last element pushed is the first to be popped.

questions.question_text: How can you implement a queue using two stacks with amortized O(1) dequeue?
options: Push to stack1, pop from stack1
Push to stack1; on dequeue, transfer all from stack1 to stack2 if stack2 is empty, then pop stack2
Alternate between stack1 and stack2 for push and pop
Use a circular buffer within a stack
questions.explanation: Each element is moved at most twice (once to stack1, once to stack2), giving amortized O(1) per operation.

questions.question_text: In an undirected graph with n vertices and no self-loops, what is the maximum number of edges?
questions.explanation: Each pair of distinct vertices can have at most one edge, giving C(n,2) = n(n-1)/2 edges.

questions.question_text: What is the space complexity of an adjacency matrix representation for a graph with V vertices?
questions.explanation: An adjacency matrix uses a V×V 2D array regardless of the number of edges, so space is O(V²).

questions.question_text: What is the time complexity of building a binary heap from an unsorted array using the bottom-up approach?
questions.explanation: The bottom-up heap construction (Floyd's algorithm) runs in O(n) because most nodes are near the bottom and require few sift-down operations.

questions.question_text: Which sorting algorithm has the best average-case time complexity?
questions.explanation: Merge Sort consistently achieves O(n log n) in all cases (best, average, worst).

questions.question_text: What is the worst-case time complexity of QuickSort?
questions.explanation: QuickSort degrades to O(n²) when the pivot consistently results in highly unbalanced partitions (e.g., already sorted input with first element as pivot).

questions.question_text: Which sorting algorithm is NOT comparison-based and can achieve O(n) time?
questions.explanation: Counting Sort uses value counting rather than comparisons, achieving O(n + k) time where k is the range of values.

questions.question_text: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array?
questions.explanation: Binary search halves the search space with each comparison, resulting in O(log n) time.

questions.question_text: When is linear search preferred over binary search?
options: When the array is very large
When the array is unsorted and searched only once
When the array is sorted in descending order
When all elements are the same
questions.explanation: Sorting first would cost O(n log n), so for a single search on unsorted data, linear O(n) search is more efficient.

questions.question_text: What are the two key properties that a problem must have for dynamic programming to be applicable?
questions.explanation: DP requires optimal substructure (optimal solution contains optimal sub-solutions) and overlapping subproblems (subproblems recur and can be cached).

questions.question_text: What is the time complexity of the dynamic programming solution for the 0/1 Knapsack problem with n items and capacity W?
questions.explanation: The DP table has n rows and W columns, each cell computed in O(1), giving O(nW) pseudo-polynomial time.

questions.question_text: Which algorithm is used for unweighted shortest path in a graph?
questions.explanation: BFS explores all neighbors level by level, naturally finding the shortest path in unweighted graphs.

questions.question_text: What is the time complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm using a binary min-heap?
questions.explanation: With a binary min-heap, each vertex extraction is O(log V) and each edge relaxation involves a decrease-key in O(log V), totaling O((V + E) log V).

questions.question_text: Which complexity class does an algorithm with runtime T(n) = 5n³ + 2n² + 10 belong to?
questions.explanation: Big-O drops constants and lower-order terms. The dominant term is n³, so T(n) = O(n³).

questions.question_text: Which algorithm design paradigm makes the locally optimal choice at each step?
questions.explanation: Greedy algorithms pick the best available option at each step without reconsidering past choices.

questions.question_text: Which problem can be solved optimally with a greedy algorithm?
questions.explanation: Activity Selection (selecting maximum non-overlapping intervals) has the greedy choice property and can be solved optimally by always picking the earliest finishing activity.

questions.question_text: What does it mean for a problem to be NP-complete?
options: It can be solved in polynomial time
It is in NP, and every NP problem can be reduced to it in polynomial time
It cannot be solved by any algorithm
questions.explanation: An NP-complete problem is both in NP (verifiable in polynomial time) and NP-hard (all NP problems reduce to it in polynomial time).

questions.question_text: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
options: Threads are always faster than processes
A thread is a lightweight unit of execution within a process that shares the process's memory space
Processes share memory while threads do not
There is no difference; they are synonyms
questions.explanation: Threads run within a process and share its heap/data segments, while each process has its own isolated address space.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a valid process state?
questions.explanation: The standard process states are New, Ready, Running, Blocked/Waiting, and Terminated. 'Compiled' is not a process state.

questions.question_text: What problem does virtual memory solve?
options: Running programs larger than physical memory
questions.explanation: Virtual memory allows processes to use more memory than physically available by paging portions to disk.

questions.question_text: In a page replacement scenario, which algorithm is theoretically optimal but impractical to implement?
questions.explanation: Bélády's optimal algorithm replaces the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future — optimal but requires future knowledge.

questions.question_text: Which CPU scheduling algorithm allocates the CPU to the process that arrived first?
questions.explanation: FCFS schedules processes in the order they arrive in the ready queue.

questions.question_text: What is the 'convoy effect' in CPU scheduling?
options: All processes finish at the same time
Short processes wait behind a long-running process in FCFS
The CPU is idle while I/O happens
Processes are scheduled in reverse order
questions.explanation: In FCFS, when a long CPU-burst process runs first, all shorter processes queue behind it, causing poor average waiting time.

questions.question_text: Which of the four Coffman conditions for deadlock involves a process holding one resource while waiting for another?
questions.explanation: Hold and Wait: a process holds at least one resource while waiting to acquire additional resources held by others.

questions.question_text: What does an inode store in a Unix-like file system?
options: File metadata (permissions, size, pointers to data blocks)
questions.explanation: An inode contains metadata about a file: ownership, permissions, timestamps, size, and pointers to data blocks — but NOT the file name.

questions.question_text: What is a semaphore used for in concurrent programming?
questions.explanation: A semaphore is a synchronization primitive that controls access to shared resources by maintaining a count of available permits.

questions.question_text: What is the key advantage of a journaling file system?
questions.explanation: Journaling file systems write changes to a log (journal) before applying them, enabling consistent recovery after crashes.

questions.question_text: Which SQL clause is used to filter rows based on a condition?
questions.explanation: The WHERE clause filters rows that satisfy a specified condition before grouping or ordering.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in SQL?
options: WHERE filters before grouping; HAVING filters after grouping
HAVING is used only with INSERT
WHERE works on aggregates; HAVING works on rows
questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before GROUP BY. HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

questions.question_text: What does Third Normal Form (3NF) eliminate?
questions.explanation: 3NF removes transitive dependencies: non-key attributes should depend only on the primary key, not on other non-key attributes.

questions.question_text: What anomaly can occur in a table that is in 2NF but not 3NF?
options: Update anomaly where changing one fact requires updating multiple rows
questions.explanation: A transitive dependency in 2NF means a fact is stored redundantly; updating it requires changing multiple rows to stay consistent.

questions.question_text: What does the 'A' in ACID properties stand for?
questions.explanation: Atomicity ensures that a transaction is treated as an indivisible unit — either all operations succeed or none do.

questions.question_text: What isolation level prevents phantom reads?
questions.explanation: Serializable is the highest isolation level and prevents phantom reads by ensuring transactions execute as if they were serial.

questions.question_text: What data structure is most commonly used for database indexes?
questions.explanation: B+ Trees are the standard for database indexes because they provide efficient range queries and ordered traversal with O(log n) lookups.

questions.question_text: Why might adding too many indexes to a table hurt performance?
options: Every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must also update all indexes, adding write overhead
Indexes speed up all operations equally
It causes the database to crash
questions.explanation: Each index must be maintained on writes. More indexes mean more overhead for INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations.

questions.question_text: In an ER diagram, what does a diamond shape represent?
questions.explanation: In ER diagrams, rectangles represent entities, ellipses represent attributes, and diamonds represent relationships.

questions.question_text: Which SQL keyword is used to combine rows from two or more tables based on a related column?
questions.explanation: JOIN combines rows from multiple tables based on a matching condition between columns.

questions.question_text: What is a weak entity in an ER model?
options: An entity with too many attributes
An entity that cannot be uniquely identified without a relationship to another entity
An entity with no primary key and no relationships
An entity that stores temporary data
questions.explanation: A weak entity depends on a strong (owner) entity for its identification, using a combination of its partial key and the owner's key.

questions.question_text: What is the main difference between TCP and UDP?
options: TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery while UDP does not guarantee delivery
UDP is used only for email
TCP uses IP addresses while UDP does not
questions.explanation: TCP is connection-oriented and guarantees reliable, ordered delivery with error checking. UDP is connectionless and trades reliability for lower latency.

questions.question_text: How many steps are in the TCP three-way handshake?
questions.explanation: The TCP three-way handshake consists of: (1) SYN from client, (2) SYN-ACK from server, (3) ACK from client.

questions.question_text: Which HTTP method is used to retrieve data from a server?
questions.explanation: GET is the HTTP method used for retrieving resources. It should be idempotent and not modify server state.

questions.question_text: What does HTTP status code 404 indicate?
questions.explanation: 404 Not Found means the server could not find the requested resource at the specified URL.

questions.question_text: What does DNS stand for and what does it do?
options: Data Network Service — manages network hardware
Domain Name System — translates domain names to IP addresses
questions.explanation: The Domain Name System translates human-readable domain names (e.g., google.com) into IP addresses that computers use to communicate.

questions.question_text: What type of DNS record maps a domain name to an IPv4 address?
questions.explanation: An A record (Address record) maps a domain name to a 32-bit IPv4 address. AAAA records map to IPv6 addresses.

questions.question_text: What does HTTPS provide that HTTP does not?
options: Encryption of data in transit via TLS/SSL
questions.explanation: HTTPS wraps HTTP communication in TLS/SSL encryption, protecting data confidentiality and integrity between client and server.

questions.question_text: What is a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack?
options: An attacker secretly intercepts and possibly alters communication between two parties
questions.explanation: In a MITM attack, an attacker positions themselves between two communicating parties, intercepting or modifying traffic without either party knowing.

questions.question_text: How many layers are in the OSI model?
questions.explanation: The OSI model has 7 layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, and Application.

questions.question_text: At which OSI layer does a router operate?
questions.explanation: Routers operate at Layer 3 (Network layer), making forwarding decisions based on IP addresses.

questions.question_text: What mechanism does TCP use to handle network congestion?
options: Congestion window (cwnd) with slow start and congestion avoidance algorithms
questions.explanation: TCP manages congestion using a congestion window that grows during slow start and reduces on packet loss, combined with congestion avoidance algorithms.

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of HTTP/2 server push?
options: The server pushes notifications to mobile devices
The server proactively sends resources to the client before the client requests them
The server forces the client to update its cache
The server redirects to another URL
questions.explanation: HTTP/2 server push allows the server to send resources (e.g., CSS, JS) proactively after receiving the initial HTML request, reducing round trips.

questions.question_text: What are the four pillars of Object-Oriented Programming?
questions.explanation: The four OOP pillars are Encapsulation (data hiding), Inheritance (code reuse), Polymorphism (many forms), and Abstraction (hiding complexity).

questions.question_text: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding?
options: Overloading: same name, different parameters in the same class; Overriding: same signature in a subclass
questions.explanation: Overloading defines multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists in the same class. Overriding redefines a parent class method in a subclass with the same signature.

questions.question_text: What is a base case in recursion?
options: The most complex case of the problem
The condition that stops the recursive calls
A case that is never reached
questions.explanation: The base case is the termination condition that stops recursion, preventing infinite recursive calls.

questions.question_text: What is tail recursion and why is it important?
options: Recursion that only works on tail elements of an array
A recursive call that is the last operation in the function, enabling compiler optimization to reuse the stack frame
Recursion that runs in reverse order
A type of recursion that doesn't need a base case
questions.explanation: In tail recursion, the recursive call is the final operation, allowing compilers to optimize it into a loop (tail call optimization), avoiding stack overflow.

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of a try-catch block?
options: To handle exceptions and prevent program crashes
questions.explanation: Try-catch provides structured exception handling: code in 'try' is monitored for errors, and 'catch' handles them gracefully.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions in Java?
options: Checked exceptions must be declared or caught at compile time; unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException) do not
questions.explanation: Checked exceptions are verified at compile time and must be handled. Unchecked exceptions (subclasses of RuntimeException) are not enforced by the compiler.

questions.question_text: Which design pattern ensures a class has only one instance and provides global access to it?
questions.explanation: The Singleton pattern restricts instantiation to a single object and provides a global access point through a static method.

questions.question_text: Which design pattern defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable?
questions.explanation: The Strategy pattern encapsulates algorithms in separate classes, allowing the client to switch between them at runtime without changing the context.

questions.question_text: What is static typing?
options: Variables never change type at runtime
Types are checked at compile time, and variables have fixed types
questions.explanation: Static typing means variable types are determined and checked at compile time. Languages like Java, C++, and TypeScript use static typing.

questions.question_text: What is type inference?
options: The compiler automatically deduces the type of a variable from its usage/initialization
A type error that is caught later
questions.explanation: Type inference allows the compiler to automatically determine variable types from context, reducing boilerplate while maintaining type safety.

questions.question_text: What is the Liskov Substitution Principle?
options: Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of a subclass without breaking the program
Only interfaces should be used, never concrete classes
Subclasses must have more methods than their parent
questions.explanation: LSP states that subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering correctness. Violating LSP creates fragile hierarchies.

questions.question_text: What is the in-order traversal sequence of a BST?
questions.explanation: In-order traversal of a BST visits left subtree, root, right subtree — producing elements in sorted ascending order.

questions.question_text: In a max-heap, where is the largest element stored?
questions.explanation: A max-heap maintains the property that every parent node is greater than or equal to its children, so the maximum is always at the root.

questions.question_text: What is the time complexity of searching in a balanced BST?
questions.explanation: A balanced BST has height O(log n), so searching follows a path from root to leaf in O(log n) time.

questions.question_text: What is a context switch and why is it considered expensive?
options: Switching between applications in a GUI
Saving and restoring process/thread state (registers, program counter, memory mappings) when the CPU switches execution — it incurs overhead from cache invalidation and state management
questions.explanation: A context switch saves the current process's state and loads another's. It is expensive due to register saves/restores, TLB flushes, and cache pollution.

questions.question_text: What is a page fault?
options: An error in the source code
An event that occurs when a program accesses a page not currently in physical memory
questions.explanation: A page fault occurs when the CPU tries to access a virtual page that isn't mapped to physical memory, triggering the OS to load it from disk.

questions.question_text: What is a dirty read in database transactions?
options: Reading data from a corrupted disk
Reading uncommitted changes made by another transaction that may later be rolled back
Reading data that is properly committed
questions.explanation: A dirty read occurs when one transaction reads data modified by another uncommitted transaction. If the other transaction rolls back, the read data becomes invalid.

questions.question_text: What is the primary purpose of a database index?
options: To speed up data retrieval operations
questions.explanation: An index creates a data structure (typically a B+ tree) that allows the database to find rows faster without scanning the entire table.

questions.question_text:
What is the output of the following Python code snippet?

```python
def transform(nums):
    return [x * 2 for x in nums if x % 2 != 0]

print(transform([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]))
```
questions.explanation: The list comprehension filters odd numbers `[1, 3, 5]` via `if x % 2 != 0` and multiplies each by 2, giving `[2, 6, 10]`.

questions.question_text:
Consider the following SQL query. What will it return?

```sql
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS emp_count
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5;
```
options: Departments where the minimum salary is 5
All departments sorted by employee count
The first 5 employees from each department
questions.explanation: `GROUP BY department` aggregates rows by department, and `HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5` filters the groups to include only those with 5 or more employees.
